arguments.content:
Listen close, you little wiggle-tails, and keep your gills shut while I speak. See that rust-caked monster half-submerged in the reeds? That is the Iron Heron. It wasn't built by a King of the Mud or a Council of Bully-Frogs. It was built by us—the scaled, the slimy, and the small.

Years ago, the Great Pike came. He didn't just eat; he demanded. He wanted every dragonfly wing and every fat beetle delivered to his hollow log. He said he owned the current. He said he was the Law of the Lake.

We didn't vote on it. We didn't wait for a general. A team of yearling toads who loved gear-turning found some brass clockwork from a sunken human ship. A group of elder pond-skaters knew the secret of the sticky-sap. They didn't ask permission; they just started building. 

They worked because they wanted to breathe free water, not because someone threatened them with a spear. The "Grease-Toads" spent weeks in the dark, fitting gears together by touch. The "Silk-Spinners" wove the external skin from reinforced spider-webs. When the Pike came to collect his tribute, he didn't find a line of submissive tadpoles. He found a thirty-foot mechanical bird with eyes of glowing phosphorus.

The Iron Heron isn't "owned" by anyone. If a gear slips today, the one who notices it fixes it. If the engine needs fuel, someone gathers the peat. We don't have a boss telling us it's time to work; we have the shared pride of knowing that mechanical beast keeps the Pike in the deeps where he belongs.

We don't hate the Pike for being a predator—that's his nature. We just don't let his nature become our cage. We are a society of builders who answer to no one but the itch in our own webbed feet and the needs of the pond we share. That Heron stands as proof: when every toad is a master of their own craft, the whole world trembles at our croak.

Now, get to the reeds. There’s a loose piston on the Heron’s left wing, and it’s not going to oil itself.
